mcqs.question: Two files in completely different directories have byte-for-byte identical content. How does git store them?
options: As the same blob object, referenced by two different tree entries
As two separate blob objects, since each has its own file path
As one blob for the content plus a separate diff for each path
Git detects the duplication and refuses to commit the second file
mcqs.explanation: Blobs are content-addressed and store no filename or path at all — identical content always hashes to the same object, and it's the tree entries (one per directory) that separately point to that one shared blob. Git doesn't store per-path diffs for blobs, nor does it block committing duplicate content.

mcqs.question: Why does cloning a repository with years of history typically transfer far less data than the sum of every historical file version?
options: Git only transfers the latest commit and fetches history lazily on demand
The server stores objects in packfiles, which delta-compress similar objects instead of storing each version in full
Old commits are automatically deleted after a retention period
Clones only include the default branch's blobs, never any historical ones
mcqs.explanation: Packfiles store many similar objects as small deltas against each other rather than full copies, which is what makes transferring deep history so much cheaper than the raw uncompressed size would suggest. A normal clone does fetch full history unless explicitly shallow, old commits aren't auto-deleted, and delta compression — not branch filtering — is the actual mechanism.

mcqs.question: A regression exists somewhere within the last 800 commits and you don't know which one introduced it. Roughly how many test cycles does `git bisect` need to find it?
options: About 800, since it must check every commit
About 400, checking every other commit
About 10, since each check halves the remaining range
Exactly 2 — the oldest good commit and the newest bad one
mcqs.explanation: Bisect performs a binary search over the commit range, halving what's left on every check, so 800 commits need roughly log₂ 800 ≈ 10 checks — dramatically fewer than a linear scan. It doesn't need to check every commit, every other commit, or just the two endpoints.

mcqs.question: A critical fix just landed on main and needs to go onto a release branch immediately, without pulling in everything else main has gained since the branches diverged. What's the right tool?
options: git rebase, replaying the entire main branch onto the release branch
git merge, combining the full history of both branches
git cherry-pick, applying just that one commit onto the release branch
git reset --hard to the fix's commit on the release branch
mcqs.explanation: Cherry-pick applies exactly one commit's diff as a new commit elsewhere, which is precisely the tool for grabbing a single fix without any of main's other unrelated changes. Rebase and merge would both bring in far more than the one commit, and reset --hard would overwrite the release branch's own history entirely rather than adding the fix to it.

mcqs.question: Why do releases typically use annotated, signed tags rather than lightweight tags?
options: Lightweight tags cannot be pushed to a remote repository
Annotated tags are required before a repository can be cloned
A signed annotated tag provides verifiable provenance — cryptographic proof of who created it and that it hasn't been altered
Lightweight tags automatically expire after 90 days
mcqs.explanation: An annotated tag is a real object that can be GPG-signed, giving downstream consumers a way to verify who cut a release and that the tag is untampered — exactly the supply-chain guarantee a lightweight tag, which is just a name pointing at a commit, can't offer. Lightweight tags push fine, aren't required for cloning, and don't expire on any schedule.

mcqs.question: A team rewrites a commit's history in their main repository, not realizing several downstream forks have pinned their merge base to that exact commit. What's the consequence for those forks?
options: Nothing — forks are entirely independent of the upstream's commit hashes
The forks automatically re-point to the new rewritten commit on their next pull
The forks' pinned commit may become unreachable once the old history is garbage-collected, breaking their ability to cleanly pull further updates
Only forks that are also submodules are affected
mcqs.explanation: A fork's merge base is a specific commit hash; if upstream rewrites that commit's history, the fork's reference to the old hash can become orphaned once garbage collection eventually prunes it, breaking clean future merges. Forks aren't automatically re-pointed by a pull, they aren't fully independent of upstream hashes they depend on, and the risk applies to any pinned reference, not only submodules specifically.
